title: Audiences & industries
examples: How do different media companies decide who their product is for?
What does it mean when a large company owns a small media outlet?
Can governments control what is shown in movies or on TV?

explain.say: Today we are looking at how media products reach people.

items: Media products are made for people.
These people are called the audience.
The audience affects how the product is made.

explain.say: Targeting means aiming a product at a specific group.
Ownership is about who controls the media product.
Regulation involves rules set by governments or bodies.
Think about a popular video game sold today.
A common mistake is thinking targeting only uses age.

items: Targeting uses more than just age.
It can use interests or income levels.

faq.q: Why do some media products seem to only appeal to one age group?
faq.a: This is because the creators are using targeting techniques. They tailor the colours, music, and themes specifically for that group.
asks: How do you make something for only kids?
Does the audience decide the style?

faq.q: If a big company owns a small newspaper, does that mean the newspaper can say anything?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Even if owned by a large company, the newspaper must still follow certain laws and regulations set by the government.
asks: Does ownership limit what they can write?
Are there limits on what big media owners can say?

faq.q: What is the difference between ownership and regulation?
faq.a: Ownership is about who legally controls the business making the media. Regulation is about the external rules that all businesses must follow.
asks: Is ownership the same as being controlled?
Do rules come from the owner or the government?

faq.q: Can governments stop a movie from being shown if they disagree with it?
faq.a: Yes, governments can regulate content by setting standards for what is acceptable to broadcast or show publicly.

faq.q: Does targeting mean you can't change the product later?
faq.a: No, targeting is a strategy used at the start. However, successful products often adapt their targeting as the audience changes over time.
asks: Can a product change its target audience?

facts: Media products are created with a specific audience in mind.
Targeting considers demographics like age and income.
Ownership refers to the legal control of the media business.
Regulation involves rules set by governing bodies.

quiz.say: A video game is designed with very bright colours and simple puzzles for young children.
quiz.why: The visual description directly shows the product is aimed at a specific group, which is the definition of targeting.

wrong.0: Regulation refers to external rules, not the internal design choices of the product.
wrong.1: Audience is the group receiving the product, not the method used to design it for them.
wrong.3: Ownership describes who owns the game company, not what the game looks like.

quiz.say: A country's government passes a law limiting the amount of violence in films shown.
quiz.why: A law passed by a government to control content is an example of regulation.

wrong.0: Targeting is about marketing the product, not setting legal limits on its content.
wrong.1: Ownership only tells us who controls the film studio, not what the law says about the film.
wrong.2: Audience is the consumer, not the body that creates the rules.

quiz.say: A small, local podcast is funded by a community trust, keeping it independent from major corporations.
quiz.why: The source of funding and control—a community trust—is discussing the ownership structure of the podcast.

wrong.0: Regulation implies external rules, whereas this describes the internal funding source.
wrong.1: The audience is the listener; the trust is the owner.
wrong.3: Targeting would describe who listens to the podcast, not who funds it.
